(a) Threads of the same process share the process address space — code, heap/data, and usually open file descriptors.
(b) Each thread keeps its own stack, registers, and program counter (its own execution context).
(c) Multithreading is lighter: creating a thread and sharing data in memory is cheaper than multiple processes plus IPC.
(d) Risk: a bad thread can overwrite shared memory and crash the whole process; you also need locks to avoid races. Separate processes isolate faults better.

Process owns the address space that sibling threads share (code + data).
Each thread has a private stack and register set.
Advantage of threads: faster context switch and easy shared-memory cooperation.
Disadvantage: no strong isolation — one thread fault can take down all threads in the process; synchronization required.

A process is a running program and threads are smaller units inside it. Threads share memory. Each thread somehow has its own workspace. Threads are faster than processes. But threads can interfere with each other.
